strengths: The combination of repulsive token interactions, symmetric attention, and recurrent parameter sharing is an interesting architectural proposal. The unconstrained energy gradients provide a useful interpretation of the symmetric attention and tied feedforward weights.

Sudoku provides the strongest empirical evidence: Hyper-SET achieves 54.70% board accuracy versus 49.30% with fewer parameters (5.20M versus 7.16M), and improves to 57.23% when inference iterations double. Results are averaged over five runs.

Experiments cover reasoning, classification, and image reconstruction, include recurrent Transformer and CRATE baselines, and investigate parameter-sharing tradeoffs. Training configurations and per-head representation diagnostics are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central constrained-optimization interpretation is not established. Equations (6) and (9) derive unconstrained gradients, but inserting RMSNorm inside those gradients does not make Equations (8) and (10) projected or Riemannian gradient updates for Equation (5). Normalizing intermediate projections does not ensure that the updated X satisfies the simultaneous constraints. Alternatively, differentiating an energy defined on normalized projections requires normalization Jacobians that are absent. Appendix C does not resolve this gap.

Descent of the combined energy is also unsupported: sequentially updating the same variables using two component energies is not automatically alternating minimization of their sum. Unconstrained, channel-wise learned step sizes further remove a general descent guarantee. Figure 4 shows empirical decreases after separately normalizing representations for energy evaluation, which does not establish optimization of the original constrained objective.

The proposed feedforward energy does not establish the claimed clustering around basis directions. For example, with D equal to the identity, every nonnegative vector on the constraint sphere minimizes Equation (4), including dense vectors far from individual basis directions. Likewise, increasing effective rank and the arccosine of mean cosine similarity does not prove isotropy, maximal hyperspherical volume, or information sufficiency. The information-bottleneck and interpretability claims therefore exceed the demonstrated results.

Important comparisons and ablations are missing. Energy Transformer is cited without a substantive experimental comparison, and established recurrent Sudoku solvers are absent. Controlled tests should isolate repulsive attention, symmetric weights, normalization, and adaptive step sizes, including whether equivalent conditioning benefits the recurrent Transformer. Current results cannot identify which proposed mechanism produces the gains.

The empirical advantage is mixed and computational efficiency is not established. The parameter-matched classification model remains below the Transformer on ImageNet-100 (55.98% versus 57.82%). Image reconstruction approaches baseline quality only after doubling recurrence and expanding the feedforward width, with FID still worse at 40% masking (45.174 versus 43.428). FLOPs, latency, memory, and matched-compute comparisons are missing.

Evidence for broader significance and reproducibility remains limited. Evaluation uses small classification datasets and partial image reconstruction, without language modeling or large-scale validation. Classification and reconstruction tables lack uncertainty estimates, making small gains difficult to assess. The step-size network is not fully specified, image augmentation details are missing, and Appendix A.3 changes conditioning from X0 to Xt without an ablation. These limitations, together with the theoretical gap, place the paper below the acceptance threshold.

Sudoku results show a meaningful improvement over the recurrent Transformer baseline: 54.70% versus 49.30% board accuracy with 5.20M versus 7.16M parameters. Accuracy further improves to 57.23% with additional inference iterations; these results are averaged over five runs.

weaknesses: The central constrained-optimization interpretation is not established. Equations (8) and (10) normalize intermediate projections before adding updates to X; they do not generally preserve the constraints in Equation (5). The derivations omit tangent-space projection or a retraction of the updated state, and would require normalization Jacobians if the intended objective instead used normalized features. Appendix C derives only the unconstrained gradients. Consequently, the implemented architecture is not shown to optimize the stated hyperspherical objective.

The joint energy-minimization claim has additional gaps. Alternating updates on two additive energy terms do not automatically decrease their sum, and unrestricted, channel-wise learned step sizes need not yield descent directions. Figure 4 measures energy after separately normalizing representations, which does not establish feasibility or descent for the actual shared state. No convergence or descent conditions bridge these gaps.

The feedforward energy does not justify the claimed clustering around basis directions. For the admissible case D = I and M = d, every nonnegative vector on the constrained sphere minimizes Equation (4), including dense vectors far from individual basis axes. Likewise, increased effective rank and an angle statistic approaching 90 degrees do not establish maximal hyperspherical volume or information sufficiency. These interpretations exceed the theoretical and empirical evidence.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed mechanisms. There are no controlled ablations of repulsion, symmetric attention, tied projections, hyperspherical normalization, or adaptive step sizes. Comparisons with CRATE are useful, but direct evaluation against Energy Transformer and stronger recurrent reasoning methods is missing. It is also unclear whether baseline Transformers receive equivalent adaptive-step conditioning.

The efficiency and performance evidence is mixed. On ImageNet-100, the parameter-matched model reaches 55.98% versus the Transformer's 57.82%. In masked image modeling, the 12-iteration model is worse on every reported metric; approaching the baseline requires 24 iterations and a substantially wider feedforward module. Parameter counts alone do not establish computational efficiency, and FLOPs, latency, and training-cost comparisons are absent.

Evaluation uncertainty and scope limit the conclusions. Classification and reconstruction results lack repeated-run uncertainty, making small gains difficult to assess. Most comparisons use single-layer recurrent models, with conventional independently parameterized depth explored only on CIFAR-10. The results support a promising compact architecture, but not yet the broad claims of competitive, interpretable Transformer design at the level expected for acceptance.

The experiments cover classification, Sudoku, and masked image reconstruction. The scaled classification model modestly outperforms the reported Transformer baseline while using fewer parameters.

The appendices provide substantial training details, additional reconstruction results, architectural variants, and representation diagnostics. Five-run reporting for selected experiments and explicit acknowledgment of computational and scalability limitations are useful.
weaknesses: The central constrained-optimization derivation is not established. Equations (9) and (11) normalize intermediate projections inside an additive update; they do not project the updated tokens onto the simultaneous constraints in Equation (6). For general learned W and D, these updates need not preserve either constraint. If the intended objective instead composes the energies with RMSNorm, its gradient requires normalization Jacobians absent from the stated updates. This directly undermines the claim that RMSNorm and the architecture emerge from solving the specified constrained problem.

The MLE foundation remains largely motivational. Appendix A rewrites an assumed expected joint log density while optimizing x, but does not specify a conditional distribution connecting the deterministic token projections to the inter-token energy in Equation (3). Nor is an equivalence or approximation bound established between the vMF likelihood and the ReLU-squared energy. The assertion following Equation (15) that maximizing a mixture likelihood equals maximizing an individual directional inner product is not generally valid.

Energy descent is not guaranteed by the implemented dynamics. The channel-wise learned step sizes are unconstrained in sign, and classification additionally conditions them on the current state. Alternating updates of two energy terms also do not automatically decrease their sum. Figure 5 provides empirical trajectories after normalization, rather than validating feasibility or descent for the stated constrained objective; its Sudoku feedforward energy initially increases. Strong claims of faithful energy minimization require substantially more justification.

The comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the proposed mechanism. Adaptive input-conditioned modulation is crucial in Table 3, but equivalent modulation is not evaluated for the Transformer and Energy Transformer baselines. Appendix F includes shared-QKV and attention-sign comparisons for representation statistics, but not corresponding task accuracies. Consequently, the gains cannot be confidently attributed to the dual-energy formulation rather than modulation, normalization, or weight tying.

Parameter efficiency is demonstrated more convincingly than computational efficiency or broad competitiveness. At equal iterations, the small model loses on two of three classification datasets and all reconstruction metrics. Near-matching reconstruction requires twice as many iterations and a substantially wider feedforward module. FLOPs, latency, memory, and compute-matched comparisons are missing, while the evaluation remains limited to small models and datasets.

The interpretation and generality claims exceed the evidence. Increased effective rank and average angle do not establish distributional uniformity, and learned directions are not empirically shown to encode identifiable semantics. Alternative energy-derived components consistently underperform the default design. Several headline tables also lack uncertainty estimates despite relatively small classification gains. These limitations, combined with the unresolved derivation issues, leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.

Equations (9) and (11) normalize intermediate projections before an unconstrained residual update; this does not preserve the simultaneous constraints in Equation (6). For example, with D equal to the identity and a positive feasible token, Equation (11) increases its norm for any positive step size. A valid projected or manifold optimization derivation is missing. If normalization is instead incorporated into the energy, its Jacobian must be accounted for.

The learned channel-wise step sizes have unrestricted signs and magnitudes, so even an otherwise correct negative-gradient direction need not remain a descent direction. Alternately updating two energy components also does not automatically decrease their sum. Figure 5 supplies empirical trends after additional normalization, rather than validating constrained descent of the actual states; its Sudoku feedforward energy initially increases. These gaps substantially weaken the claim of an architecture obtained through pure energy minimization.

The MLE argument is largely motivational. Appendix A rewrites an assumed expected log joint density while optimizing the representation x, but does not specify a conditional density whose KL divergence yields the proposed inter-token energy. Deterministic projections do not themselves define the required continuous conditional distributions. Likewise, the squared-ReLU energy is introduced as a surrogate without establishing its relationship to the vMF mixture likelihood. The claimed probabilistic foundation therefore does not derive the implemented objective.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed energy structure from the substantial adaptive modulation network. Table 3 shows strong dependence on learned step sizes, but there is no matched Transformer baseline equipped with the same input- and iteration-conditioned modulation. Appendix D.3 also changes conditioning from the initial state to the current state for classification. Controlled task-performance ablations of modulation, normalization, symmetry, and weight tying are needed to attribute the gains.

Parameter efficiency is demonstrated more convincingly than computational efficiency or broad competitiveness. Most comparisons use shared-layer recurrent baselines, with limited comparison against independently tuned conventional architectures. No FLOPs, latency, or training-time measurements are reported. Image reconstruction requires twice as many iterations and a wider feedforward module to approach the baseline, and still trails on several metrics. Small classification improvements frequently lack reported uncertainty.

The interpretability and generality claims exceed the evidence. Effective rank and average cosine-derived angles do not establish hyperspherical uniformity or semantic meaning of the learned bases. The architectural relationship to Energy Transformer, CRATE, and existing depth-wise LoRA methods needs sharper differentiation, especially because the strongest claimed distinction is a rigorous optimization interpretation that remains unresolved. These issues outweigh the promising empirical results at a selective conference.

Sudoku results are promising: Hyper-SET achieves 54.70% board accuracy versus 49.30% for the recurrent Transformer with fewer parameters, and improves to 57.23% with additional inference iterations. Results are averaged over five runs.

The scaled classification model achieves useful parameter–accuracy trade-offs across three datasets. Comparisons include relevant energy-based architectures, and the paper investigates layer sharing, alternative operators, and depth-wise LoRA.

The appendices provide substantial configuration details and additional experiments. Energy trajectories and representation statistics help examine the proposed mechanism, and the limitations section acknowledges computational overhead and restricted scalability.
weaknesses: The central constrained-optimization derivation is not established. Equations (9) and (11) normalize projected features inside residual updates, but do not project the updated tokens onto the simultaneous constraints in Equation (6). For general learned W and D, this does not preserve feasibility. Alternatively, interpreting the energy as a function of normalized projections requires normalization Jacobians that are absent from the updates. Thus the claimed emergence of RMSNorm from faithful constrained energy minimization has a substantive technical gap.

Energy descent is not guaranteed by the implemented dynamics. Step sizes are unconstrained, channel-wise learned vectors, and sequential updates to the two energy terms need not decrease their sum. Figure 5 evaluates energies after additional normalization, so it does not resolve the mismatch with the stated constrained objective. These observations support an empirical energy-inspired interpretation, but not the stronger claims of pure energy minimization or preserved descent under extrapolation.

The connection from maximum likelihood to the actual architecture remains heuristic. Appendix A rewrites an assumed probabilistic objective, but does not specify a conditional density whose KL divergence yields the token-interaction energy, or establish how squared-ReLU energy approximates the stated von Mises–Fisher mixture. Deterministic projections are also not reconciled with the conditional distributions. Moreover, with D equal to the identity, Equation (5) is constant throughout the positive orthant of the constrained sphere, so it need not select individual semantic directions.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the contribution of the energy formulation. Adaptive step sizes have a very large effect in Table 3, yet task-accuracy comparisons against Transformers and Energy Transformer equipped with the same modulation mechanism are missing. Shared-QKV controls in Appendix F report representation statistics rather than downstream accuracy. Identical training settings alone do not establish that the poorly performing competing architectures received appropriate tuning.

Parameter efficiency is better supported than computational efficiency or broad superiority. At equal iterations, masked reconstruction is worse on every reported metric; approaching the baseline requires doubling iterations and substantially widening the feedforward module. FLOPs, latency, and memory comparisons are absent. Most experiments use recurrent single-layer baselines, with only a limited untied-depth comparison, restricting conclusions about standard Transformers.

The evidence for generality and interpretability is limited. Evaluation covers Sudoku and relatively small vision benchmarks, with no language modeling or large-scale validation. Most tabulated gains lack uncertainty estimates, including modest classification and LoRA improvements. Increased effective rank and average angle do not establish distributional uniformity or semantic alignment, and the alternative energy-derived operators consistently underperform the primary design. Together with the central derivation gaps, these limitations leave the paper below the acceptance threshold.
